Whether dishwater can be used to water plants is a genuinely contested question, with sources offering conflicting guidance. Some official sources actively recommend it: Southern Water [d7] advises gardeners to "re-use dishwater or water used to boil vegetables or pasta, and fill a watering can instead," and a Georgia city government source [d8] states "Save dishwater and bathwater for watering plants... The soap isn't harmful. In fact, it kills aphids and other plant-destroying insects." Similarly, d1 argues that "the detergent residue in the water won't hurt them," provided the soap contains no boron or bleach, and d2 and d4 present numerous anecdotal accounts of successful dishwater use in gardens. However, other sources take a more cautious or opposing stance: Penn State Extension [d6] explicitly states that "in Pennsylvania, we cannot use water that has been in contact with people (bath water, shower water, or dishwater) to water our plants," and d9 warns that "the chemicals and bleach in gray-water hinders the ability of plants to soak in nutrition and may contaminate the water table." Public health officials cited in d5 recommend dishwater "only when fresh water isn't available," and caution that it can attract pests, cause root rot, and harm plants if the water contains bleach or high sodium from water softeners. Forum contributors in d3 also raise concerns about food residues, fats, salts, and detergent chemicals leaching into the water table, even as others in the same thread report no harm to plants during drought use.
